{{Short description|Fluid dynamics process driving mixing in the oceans}}

[[File:Internal wave breaking in the Rainbow Ridge.jpg|thumb|Temporal evolution of internal wave breaking in the Rainbow Ridge, part of the [[Mid-Atlantic Ridge]], North Atlantic Ocean. Measurements were taken by a single [[mooring]] deployed from June 28th till July 10th 2016. When the internal wave encounters the steep topography of the ridge, it breaks at around 1200 seconds and causes mixing and dissipation of heat. Modified from van Haren, et al. (2017)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van Haren |first1=Hans |last2=Duineveld |first2=Gerard |last3=de Stigter |first3=Henko |date=2017-09-28 |title=Prefrontal bore mixing: Prefrontal Bore Mixing |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/2017GL074384 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |language=en |volume=44 |issue=18 |pages=9408–9415 |doi=10.1002/2017GL074384|s2cid=134994034 }}</ref>|440x440px]]

'''Internal wave breaking''' is a process during which [[Internal wave|internal gravity waves]] attain a large amplitude compared to their [[length scale]], become [[Nonlinear system|nonlinearly]] unstable and finally break. This process is accompanied by turbulent dissipation and mixing. As internal gravity waves carry energy and momentum from the environment of their inception, breaking and subsequent [[Turbulence|turbulent]] mixing affects the fluid characteristics in locations of breaking. Consequently, internal wave breaking influences even the large scale flows and composition in both the ocean and the atmosphere. In the atmosphere, momentum deposition by internal wave breaking plays a key role in atmospheric phenomena such as the [[Quasi-biennial oscillation|Quasi-Biennial Oscillation]] and the [[Brewer–Dobson circulation|Brewer-Dobson Circulation]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pisoft |first1=P. |last2=Šácha |first2=P. |last3=Jacobi |first3=C. |last4=Lilienthal |first4=F. |date=2015-12-01 |title=Model Study of IGW Hotspot Implications for the Middle Atmospheric Dynamics and Transport |journal=AGU Fall Meeting Abstracts |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015AGUFMSA13A2336P |volume=2015 |pages=SA13A–2336|bibcode=2015AGUFMSA13A2336P }}</ref> In the deep ocean, mixing induced by internal wave breaking is an important driver of the [[Thermohaline circulation|meridional overturning circulation]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nikurashin |first1=Maxim |last2=Ferrari |first2=Raffaele |date=2013-06-21 |title=Overturning circulation driven by breaking internal waves in the deep ocean |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=40 |issue=12 |pages=3133–3137 |doi=10.1002/grl.50542 |bibcode=2013GeoRL..40.3133N |s2cid=16754887 |issn=0094-8276|doi-access=free |hdl=1721.1/85568 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> On smaller scales, breaking-induced mixing is important for [[sediment transport]] and for nutrient supply to the [[photic zone]].<ref name="Melissa M 2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Omand |first1=Melissa M. |last2=Leichter |first2=James J. |last3=Franks |first3=Peter J. S. |last4=Guza |first4=R. T. |last5=Lucas |first5=Andrew J. |last6=Feddersen |first6=Falk |date=2011-03-31 |title=Physical and biological processes underlying the sudden surface appearance of a red tide in the nearshore |journal=Limnology and Oceanography |volume=56 |issue=3 |pages=787–801 |doi=10.4319/lo.2011.56.3.0787 |bibcode=2011LimOc..56..787O |s2cid=86615463 |issn=0024-3590|doi-access=free }}</ref> Most breaking of oceanic internal waves occurs in [[Continental shelf|continental shelves]], well below the ocean surface, which makes it a difficult phenomenon to observe.

The contribution of breaking internal waves to many atmospheric and ocean processes makes it important to [[Parametrization (atmospheric modeling)|parametrize]] their effects in [[Numerical weather prediction|weather]] and [[climate model]]s.

== Breaking mechanisms ==
Similar to what happens to surface gravity waves near a coastline, when internal waves enter shallow waters and encounter steep [[topography]], they steepen and grow in amplitude in a [[Wave nonlinearity|nonlinear]] process known as [[Wave shoaling|shoaling]]. As the wave travels over topography with increasing height, bed friction leads to internal waves becoming asymmetrical with an increasing steepness. These nonlinear internal waves on a shallow slope are generally referred to as internal bores.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last1=Masunaga |first1=Eiji |title=Internal Wave Breaking Dynamics and Associated Mixing in the Coastal Ocean |date=2019-01-01 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780124095489109534 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Ocean Sciences (Third Edition) |pages=548–554 |editor-last=Cochran |editor-first=J. Kirk |place=Oxford |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |isbn=978-0-12-813082-7 |access-date=2022-03-20 |last2=Arthur |first2=Robert S. |last3=Fringer |first3=Oliver B. |editor2-last=Bokuniewicz |editor2-first=Henry J. |editor3-last=Yager |editor3-first=Patricia L.}}</ref> Wave height and energy increase until a critical steepness is reached, whereafter the wave breaks by [[Convective instability|convective]], [[Kelvin–Helmholtz instability|Kelvin-Helmholtz]] or parametric subharmonic instability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=SMYTH |first1=WILLIAM D. |last2=MOUM |first2=JAMES N. |date=2012 |title=Ocean Mixing by Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability |journal=Oceanography |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=140–149 |doi=10.5670/oceanog.2012.49 |jstor=24861351 |issn=1042-8275|doi-access=free }}</ref> Due to the relatively small density differences (and thus small restoring forces) over the ocean depth, ocean internal waves may reach amplitudes up to around 100 m.<ref name=":0" /> Analogous to surface wave breaking in the region known as the [[surf zone]], internal breaking waves dissipate energy in what is known as the ''internal surf zone.''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sinnett |first1=Gregory |last2=Feddersen |first2=Falk |last3=Lucas |first3=Andrew J. |last4=Pawlak |first4=Geno |last5=Terrill |first5=Eric |date=2018-03-01 |title=Observations of Nonlinear Internal Wave Run-Up to the Surfzone |url=https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/phoc/48/3/jpo-d-17-0210.1.xml |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |language=EN |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=531–554 |doi=10.1175/JPO-D-17-0210.1 |bibcode=2018JPO....48..531S |issn=0022-3670}}</ref>

=== Internal tide breaking ===
[[Internal tide|Internal tidal waves]] are internal waves at [[Theory of tides|tidal frequency]] in the ocean, which are generated by the interaction of the tide with the ocean topography. Alongside internal [[inertial wave]]s, they constitute the majority of the ocean internal wavefield. The internal tides consist of so-called ''low modes'' and ''high modes'' with varying vertical wavelengths. As these waves propagate, the high modes tend to dissipate their energy quickly, leading to the low modes to dominate further away from the location of their generation.<ref name=":0" /> Low mode internal waves, with wavelengths exceeding 100&nbsp;km, generated by either tides or winds acting on the sea surface, can travel thousands of kilometers from their regions of generation, where they will eventually encounter sloping topography and break.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=SIMMONS |first1=HARPER L. |last2=ALFORD |first2=MATTHEW H. |date=2012 |title=Simulating the Long-Range Swell of Internal Waves Generated by Ocean Storms |journal=Oceanography |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=30–41 |doi=10.5670/oceanog.2012.39 |jstor=24861341 |issn=1042-8275|doi-access=free }}</ref> When this happens, [[isopycnal]]s become steeper and steeper, where the wavefront is followed by a sharp temperature drop. This then leads to an unstable density profile that eventually overturns and breaks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Martini |first1=Kim I. |last2=Alford |first2=Matthew H. |last3=Kunze |first3=Eric |last4=Kelly |first4=Samuel M. |last5=Nash |first5=Jonathan D. |date=2013-01-01 |title=Internal Bores and Breaking Internal Tides on the Oregon Continental Slope |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |language=EN |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=120–139 |doi=10.1175/JPO-D-12-030.1 |bibcode=2013JPO....43..120M |issn=0022-3670|doi-access=free }}</ref> The magnitude of the topographic slope and the slope of the internal wave beam dictate where internal waves break.

The slope of an internal wave beam (<math>r</math>) can be expressed as the ratio between its horizontal (<math>k</math>'')'' and vertical (<math>m</math>) wavenumbers:<ref name=":0" />

<math>r = \Bigg| \frac{k}{m} \Bigg| = \sqrt{\frac{\omega^2-f^2}{N^2-\omega^2}}</math>

where <math>N</math> is the [[Brunt–Väisälä frequency|buoyancy frequency]] (or [[Brunt-Väisälä frequency]]), <math>f</math> is the [[Coriolis frequency]] and <math>\omega</math> is the wave frequency in the dispersion relation that governs the propagation of internal waves in a continuously stratified and rotating medium:

<math>\omega^2 = \frac{N^2k^2 + f^2m^2}{k^2+m^2}</math>.

In the case that the slope of a downgoing incident internal wave beam is larger than the topographic slope (''supercritical'' slope), waves will be reflected downward. In the case that the slope of a downgoing incident internal wave beam is smaller than the topographic slope (''subcritical'' slope), however, waves will be reflected upward with reduced wavelength and lower [[group velocity]]. Because the energy flux is conserved during reflection, energy density and therefore wave amplitude in the reflected wave must increase with respect to the incident wave.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eriksen |first=Charles C. |date=1985-09-01 |title=Implications of Ocean Bottom Reflection for Internal Wave Spectra and Mixing |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |language=EN |volume=15 |issue=9 |pages=1145–1156 |doi=10.1175/1520-0485(1985)015<1145:IOOBRF>2.0.CO;2 |bibcode=1985JPO....15.1145E |issn=0022-3670|doi-access=free }}</ref> This increase in amplitude and wave steepness results in the waves being subject to breaking. These effects are increased the closer the slope of the internal wave beam is to the magnitude of the topographic slope. When the slope of the beam of the incoming internal wave is equal to the topographic slope, the slope of the topography is referred to as the ''critical'' slope. Critical slopes and near-critical slopes are important locations for both wave breaking and wave generation via tide-topography interactions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lamb |first=Kevin G. |date=2014-01-03 |title=Internal Wave Breaking and Dissipation Mechanisms on the Continental Slope/Shelf |journal=Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics |language=en |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=231–254 |doi=10.1146/annurev-fluid-011212-140701 |bibcode=2014AnRFM..46..231L |issn=0066-4189|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Internal solitary wave breaking ===
Owing to the generally long distances traveled by internal tidal waves, they may steepen and form trains of internal solitary waves, or internal [[soliton]]s.<ref name=":0" /> These internal solitons have much shorter wavelengths, on the order of hundreds of meters, making them much steeper than internal tides. The ratio of the topographic slope to the wave steepness can be characterized by the internal [[Iribarren number]]:

<math>\xi = \frac{s}{\sqrt{a/\lambda}}</math>

where <math>s</math> is the topographical slope, <math>a</math> the internal wave amplitude and <math>\lambda</math> the wavelength of the internal wave. The internal Iribarren number can be used to classify internal bores into two categories: ''canonical bores'' and ''non-canonical bores''. For a gentle slope, as is typical for the [[continental shelf]] and nearshore areas, the internal Iribarren number is low (<math>\xi  << 1</math>) such that canonical bores occur. In this case, an incoming internal solitary wave can convert to a packet of solitary waves or boluses as it travels up the slope in a process referred to as fission. This is also called a fission breaker. Canonical bores are generally accompanied by an intense drop in temperature as the wavefront passes by, followed by a gradual increase over time.<ref name=":0" />

In rarer cases, non-canonical (<math>\xi = O (1)</math>) bores may occur. In these cases, for an increasing internal Iribarren number (that is, steeper waves or steeper topographic slope), wave breaking can be classified successively as surging, collapsing and plunging breakers (see [[Breaking wave]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nakayama |first1=Keisuke |last2=Sato |first2=Takahiro |last3=Shimizu |first3=Kenji |last4=Boegman |first4=Leon |date=2019-01-02 |title=Classification of internal solitary wave breaking over a slope |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevFluids.4.014801 |journal=Physical Review Fluids |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=014801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevFluids.4.014801|bibcode=2019PhRvF...4a4801N |hdl=20.500.14094/90006650 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Contrary to canonical bores, temperature gradually decreases as the wavefront passes by, followed by a sharp increase in temperature. Due to the steeper topographic slopes associated with non-canonical bores, a larger part of the wave energy is reflected back, meaning there is less turbulent energy that leads to mixing.<ref name=":0" />

== Mixing ==
Breaking internal waves are regarded to play an important role on mixing of the ocean based on lab experiments and remote sensing. The effect of internal waves on mixing is also studied extensively in [[direct numerical simulation]]s. Even though research indicates that internal wave breaking is important for local turbulence, there remains uncertainty in global estimates.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Klymak |first1=Jody |last2=Legg |first2=Sonya |author-link2=Sonya Legg |last3=Alford |first3=Matthew |last4=Buijsman |first4=Maarten |last5=Pinkel |first5=Robert |last6=Nash |first6=Jonathan |date=2012-06-01 |title=The Direct Breaking of Internal Waves at Steep Topography |journal=Oceanography |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=150–159 |doi=10.5670/oceanog.2012.50 |issn=1042-8275|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Arthur |first1=R. |last2=Fringer |first2=O. |date=2014 |title=The dynamics of breaking internal solitary waves on slopes |journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics |volume=761 |pages=360–398 |doi=10.1017/jfm.2014.641|bibcode=2014JFM...761..360A |s2cid=37573503 }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Bourgault |first1=D. |last2=Blokhina |first2=M. D. |last3=Mirshak |first3=R. |last4=Kelley |first4=D. E. |date=2007-02-02 |title=Evolution of a shoaling internal solitary wavetrain |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=34 |issue=3 |doi=10.1029/2006gl028462 |bibcode=2007GeoRL..34.3601B |s2cid=55295073 |issn=0094-8276|doi-access= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arthur |first1=Robert S. |last2=Koseff |first2=Jeffrey R. |last3=Fringer |first3=Oliver B. |date=March 2017 |title=Local versus volume-integrated turbulence and mixing in breaking internal waves on slopes |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/abs/local-versus-volumeintegrated-turbulence-and-mixing-in-breaking-internal-waves-on-slopes/755C318BBDB1DDD448EC3ACE18ADC4CD |journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics |language=en |volume=815 |pages=169–198 |doi=10.1017/jfm.2017.36 |bibcode=2017JFM...815..169A |s2cid=85561732 |issn=0022-1120|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Breaking internal tidal waves can result in turbulent water columns of several hundred meters high and the [[Turbulence kinetic energy|turbulent kinetic energy]] may reach levels up to 10.000 times higher than in the open ocean.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

=== Quantifying mixing efficiency ===
The intensity of the turbulence caused by breaking internal waves depends mainly on the ratio between topographical steepness and the wave steepness, known as the internal Iribarren number. A smaller internal Iribarren number correlates with a larger intensity of the resulting turbulence due to internal wave breaking. That means that a small internal Iribarren number predicts that a lot of the wave energy will be transferred to mixing and turbulence, while a large internal Iribarren number predicts that the wave energy will reflect offshore.<ref name=":0" />

Studies express the mixing efficiency as the ratio between the total amount of mixing and the total irreversible energy loss. In other words, the mixing efficiency can generally be defined as the following ratio:

<math>\gamma = \frac{\Delta V}{E}</math>,

where <math>\gamma</math> is the mixing efficiency, <math>\Delta V</math> the change in background potential energy due to mixing and <math>E</math> the total energy expended. Because <math>\Delta V</math> and <math>E</math> are not directly observable, studies use different definitions to determine the mixing efficiency.

It is notoriously hard to estimate the mixing efficiency in the ocean, due to practical limitations in measuring [[ocean dynamics]]. Besides measurements of ocean dynamics, the mixing efficiency can also be obtained from lab experiments and numerical simulations, but they also have their limitations. Therefore, these three different approaches have slightly different definitions of mixing efficiency. In theory these three approaches should give the same estimates for the mixing efficiency, but there remain discrepancies between them. Therefore, there are varying estimates and disagreements on mixing efficiency and comparisons are difficult due to the different definitions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gregg |first1=M.C. |last2=D'Asaro |first2=E.A. |last3=Riley |first3=J.J. |last4=Kunze |first4=E. |date=2018-01-03 |title=Mixing Efficiency in the Ocean |journal=Annual Review of Marine Science |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=443–473 |doi=10.1146/annurev-marine-121916-063643 |pmid=28934598 |bibcode=2018ARMS...10..443G |issn=1941-1405}}</ref>

Studies that quantify the mixing properties of breaking internal solitary waves have split estimates of the mixing efficiency range, with values between 5% and 25% for laboratory experiments<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Michallet |first1=H. |last2=Ivey |first2=G. N. |date=1999-06-15 |title=Experiments on mixing due to internal solitary waves breaking on uniform slopes |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans |volume=104 |issue=C6 |pages=13467–13477 |doi=10.1029/1999jc900037 |bibcode=1999JGR...10413467M |issn=0148-0227|doi-access=free }}</ref> or between 13% and 21% for numerical simulations<ref name=":2" /> depending on the Internal Iribarren number.

=== Mass and sediment transport ===
Breaking and shoaling of internal waves have been shown to cause the transport of mass and energy in the form of sediment and heat, but also of nutrients, [[plankton]] and other forms of marine life.

==== Sediment transport ====
Wave breaking causes mass and sediment transport that is important for the ocean biology and shaping of the [[Continental shelf|continental shelves]] due to [[erosion]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Pomar |first1=L. |last2=Morsilli |first2=M. |last3=Hallock |first3=P. |last4=Bádenas |first4=B. |date=2012-02-01 |title=Internal waves, an under-explored source of turbulence events in the sedimentary record |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012825211001784 |journal=Earth-Science Reviews |language=en |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=56–81 |doi=10.1016/j.earscirev.2011.12.005 |bibcode=2012ESRv..111...56P |issn=0012-8252|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The erosion caused by internal wave breaking can result in sediment to be suspended and transported off-shore. This off-shore sediment transport may give rise to the emergence of [[nepheloid layer]]s, which are in turn important for the ocean biology.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":0" /> Direct numerical simulations show that breaking internal waves are also responsible for on-shore sediment transport, after which sediment can be deposited or transported elsewhere.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oliver Fringer |url=https://web.stanford.edu/~fringer/research_iwaves.html |access-date=2022-03-24 |website=web.stanford.edu}}</ref>

Although many studies show that internal wave breaking leads to sediment transport, their traces in the [[geologic record]] remain uncertain. Their [[sedimentary structures]] may coexist in [[turbidite]]s on continental slopes and canyons.<ref name=":4" />

==== Transport of nutrients ====
The mixing and transport of nutrients in the ocean is affected largely by internal wave breaking. The arrival of internal tidal bores has been shown to cause a 10 to 40 fold increase of nutrients on [[Conch Reef]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leichter |first1=James J. |last2=Stewart |first2=Hannah L. |last3=Miller |first3=Steven L. |date=July 2003 |title=Episodic nutrient transport to Florida coral reefs |url=https://aslopubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.4319/lo.2003.48.4.1394 |journal=Limnology and Oceanography |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=1394–1407 |doi=10.4319/lo.2003.48.4.1394  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2003LimOc..48.1394L |s2cid=15125174 |issn=0024-3590|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Here it has been shown that the appearance of internal bores provide a predictable and periodic source of transport that can be important for a diversity of marine life.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leichter |first1=Jj |last2=Shellenbarger |first2=G |last3=Genovese |first3=Sj |last4=Wing |first4=Sr |date=1998 |title=Breaking internal waves on a Florida (USA) coral reef:a plankton pump at work? |url=http://www.int-res.com/abstracts/meps/v166/p83-97/ |journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series |language=en |volume=166 |pages=83–97 |doi=10.3354/meps166083 |bibcode=1998MEPS..166...83L |issn=0171-8630|doi-access=free }}</ref> Large amplitude tidal internal tidal waves can cause sediments to be resuspended for as long as 5 hours each tidal wave<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Butman |first1=B. |last2=Alexander |first2=P. S. |last3=Scotti |first3=A. |last4=Beardsley |first4=R. C. |last5=Anderson |first5=S. P. |date=2006-11-01 |title=Large internal waves in Massachusetts Bay transport sediments offshore |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278434306002329 |journal=Continental Shelf Research |series=Special Issue in Honor of Richard W. Sternberg's Contributions to Marine Sedimentology |language=en |volume=26 |issue=17 |pages=2029–2049 |doi=10.1016/j.csr.2006.07.022 |bibcode=2006CSR....26.2029B |hdl=1912/1625 |issn=0278-4343|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and internal bores have shown to play a vital role in the onshore transportation of planktonic larvae.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pineda |first=Jesús |date=1991-08-02 |title=Predictable Upwelling and the Shoreward Transport of Planktonic Larvae by Internal Tidal Bores |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.253.5019.548 |journal=Science |volume=253 |issue=5019 |pages=548–549 |doi=10.1126/science.253.5019.548 |pmid=17745188 |bibcode=1991Sci...253..548P |s2cid=21256893 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Internal wave breaking may also cause ecological hazards, such as [[red tide]]s<ref name="Melissa M 2011"/> and low dissolved oxygen levels.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Booth |first1=J. Ashley T. |last2=McPhee-Shaw |first2=Erika E. |last3=Chua |first3=Paul |last4=Kingsley |first4=Eric |last5=Denny |first5=Mark |last6=Phillips |first6=Roger |last7=Bograd |first7=Steven J. |last8=Zeidberg |first8=Louis D. |last9=Gilly |first9=William F. |date=2012-08-15 |title=Natural intrusions of hypoxic, low pH water into nearshore marine environments on the California coast |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278434312001653 |journal=Continental Shelf Research |language=en |volume=45 |pages=108–115 |doi=10.1016/j.csr.2012.06.009 |bibcode=2012CSR....45..108B |issn=0278-4343|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
